To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) distributional similarity can help learning referential word meanings, (2) this effect is stronger for certain words, (3) the effect is stronger for some image datasets than others.

(i) the distributional similarity of words to other words is not a good proxy of the similarity of the objects they refer to; (ii) the similarity of the referents is more important than the similarity of the words; and (iii) the similarity of words to their referents is not a good predictor of the similarity of words.

for some referential words, distributional similarity information helps to improve their visual predictors, but that this is not the case for all word meanings, and that this effect is not limited to the most basic level of the taxonomy, but can be seen for hypernyms as well.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much distributional similarity information we can use to learn the meaning of referential words.
the question of how much distributional information can help to learn referential word meanings, and which words benefit the most from this kind of information.
the question of how to learn better visual representations of referential words from images and text.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the contribution of distributional similarity to learning referential word meanings depends on the type of word, and that the effect is strongest for words with high frequency of occurrence in text.
distributional similarity is not always helpful, but it can be helpful in the right circumstances.
distributional information does indeed help for some words, while it hurts for other ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
distributional similarity can be a powerful source of information, but it has to be used carefully and selectively.

distributional similarity information is a valuable addition to the learning setup, but only when it is not too costly to compute, i.e. when there are only a small number of semantically similar words to a given referent.
distributional similarity is not a panacea for all words, but that it is an important factor in the acquisition of referential word meanings for certain words.
The main takeaway from our work is that

distributional similarity information should not be used blindly, as it may have a detrimental effect in certain circumstances, and that the choice of the learning setup should be informed by a priori knowledge of the words’ meanings.
distributional similarity information is not a universal panacea to improving visual word predictors, but rather a powerful tool for specific words and tasks.
we can improve visual object detectors by exploiting distributional semantic information during training.
